teaser: Every page now costs a few pence from £5 of credit kept in your browser, and the reading history it keeps is what personalises the site.
core_idea: A reading meter that lives only in the browser, a few pence a page from five pounds of starting credit with a simulated top-up and no blocking, tests whether people would pay a little for reading when what they get back is a site that personalises itself from a history nobody else holds; escaping the meter is easy, but escaping it also discards the history, which is the point of the experiment.

nodes.label: A meter in the browser
nodes.summary: Every page priced in pence, debited from £5.00 of credit kept in localStorage; one debit per page per visit.

nodes.label: Never block a page
nodes.summary: Out of credit, the page is shown and the read recorded as unpaid, with an offer to top up.

nodes.label: Every step but the payment
nodes.summary: Packs, a cart, a review, a confirm and a receipt; credit added at once, nothing charged.

nodes.label: The history is the product
nodes.summary: The ledger of what was read, with topics, is enough to pick unread articles for the reader.

nodes.label: The meter can be escaped; the personalisation cannot be copied
nodes.summary: A private window starts again at £5.00 and with no history.

nodes.label: Would people pay for a site that knows them?
nodes.summary: The experiment the meter puts in front of a reader.

nodes.label: The pt.newsroom wallet
nodes.summary: One cent a page, a self-refilling five-euro wallet, a ledger page: the first version.

nodes.label: 402 Payment Required
nodes.summary: Reserved in the web's protocol in 1997 for micropayments, still unused.

quotes.text: The meter can be escaped; the personalisation cannot be copied.
quotes.why: The trade the experiment puts in front of a reader.

quotes.text: The history never leaves the machine it was made on.
quotes.why: Personalisation without an account, a cookie banner or a server.
